claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is compositionally complex and single-phase.
Arc melting followed by homogenization produces a uniform microstructure with no detectable secondary phases.
The initial alloy exhibits excellent ductility.
Small amounts of element-specific segregation can develop during service or controlled thermal exposure.
Controlled aging near 800°C can accelerate grain-boundary segregation without causing gross grain coarsening.
Segregation-driven local compositional fluctuations produce nanoscale intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries.
Elements with a high propensity for intermetallic formation become locally enriched at grain boundaries during thermal aging.
Grain-boundary enrichment initiates nanoscale intermetallic precipitation.
Nanoscale grain-boundary precipitation lowers grain-boundary cohesive strength.
The nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates act as crack-initiation sites.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion and precipitate-assisted crack initiation promote brittle intergranular fracture.
The unaged alloy fails predominantly through transgranular, ductile fracture mechanisms.
Thermally aged specimens will have lower fracture toughness than unaged baseline specimens.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit more intergranular fracture than unaged baseline specimens.
The proposed comparison uses otherwise nearly identical aged and unaged sample sets tested under identical room-temperature monotonic fracture-toughness conditions.
The hypothesized behavior is bounded to moderate thermal exposure near 800°C followed by mechanical loading at or near room temperature.
The alloy remains compositionally complex and single-phase in the bulk after the relevant exposure.
Segregation kinetics and the critical concentration for embrittling intermetallic formation depend on minor alloying additions and processing history.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as homogenized, but the comparison state is repeatedly called 'as-solidified' or 'as-solidified, homogenized.' Homogenization is a post-solidification treatment, so the baseline state is defined inconsistently.
